```{r}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
set_theme(theme_bw(16))
```

## Choose our parameters

```{r}
beta_0 <-  10 # Intercept
beta_1 <-  0.1 # Additional typo per increase in typing speed
beta_2 <- -10 # Difference between typist B and the reference level (A)
sigma <- 3 # Standard deviation of the residuals
```

## Generate our predictors

Remember, for Simpson's paradox, there must be a correlation between the predictors.

```{r}
# Sample size
N <- 30
# Typist identities
typist <- sample(c("A","B"), N, replace = TRUE)
# Dummy variable for typist B
typistB <-  ifelse(typist == "B", 1, 0)

# THIS IS THE KEY PART
typing_speed <- rnorm(N, mean = ifelse(typist == "B", 100, 45), sd = 15)
```

## Calculate the expected value of the response

```{r}
expected_typos <-  beta_0 + beta_1 * typing_speed + beta_2 * typistB
```

## Simulate the response variable


```{r}
typos <- rnorm(n = N,
            mean = expected_typos,
            sd = sigma)
```

## Visualize!


```{r}
simulated_typing <- tibble(typing_speed, typos, typist)

ggplot(simulated_typing, aes(typing_speed, typos, fill = typist)) +
    # Shape 21 is a hollow circle that can be filled
    geom_point(size = 2, shape = 21)
```

## Fit and interpret

If we only look at typing speed:


```{r}
one_predictor_lm <- lm(typos ~ typing_speed, simulated_typing)
summary(one_predictor_lm)
```

If we look at both typind speed AND the typist:


```{r}
two_predictor_lm <- lm(typos ~ typing_speed + typist, simulated_typing)
summary(two_predictor_lm)
```
